statement: A long strip of paper is folded in half, then in half again, then in half a third time, each fold bringing the two ends together. One straight cut is then made across the middle of the folded strip, at right angles to its length, through all the layers. Into how many pieces does the paper fall?

choices.misconception: I thought one straight cut always makes two pieces, however many layers it passes through.
I thought each fold adds just one extra piece, so one cut and three folds give 1 + 3 = 4.
I counted the 8 layers the scissors pass through and took each layer as one piece.
I thought each of the 8 layers is cut into two separate pieces, giving 8 x 2.

hints: Count how many cuts the unfolded strip actually receives.
Three folds stack 8 layers, so the single cut slices the long strip at 8 different places. A strip cut at several places falls into one more piece than there are cuts, just like a ribbon.
Unfolded, the strip has 8 separate cuts along its length.

solutions.reliable: Folding in half three times stacks 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 layers. The cut goes through every layer, so the unfolded strip is cut at 8 different places along its length. A strip cut at 8 places falls into 8 + 1 = 9 pieces; most of them are folded loops that stay in one piece because they are joined at a fold. The transferable idea: unfold in your head and count the cuts on the flat strip, then pieces = cuts + 1.
solutions.elegant: Try small cases. One fold: 2 layers, 2 cuts, 3 pieces. Two folds: 4 cuts, 5 pieces. The pieces are always the layers plus 1, so three folds give 8 + 1 = 9.

whyOnTest: Folding-and-cutting questions reward unfolding in your head and counting cuts on the flat strip, not layers in the stack.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
